title: Raw NL2SQL vs Ontology-Grounded: The Same Question, Two Paths
purpose: Contrast a business question answered by NL2SQL against a raw star-schema table structure with the same question answered through a Fabric IQ ontology — showing exactly where each path's understanding of 'what a customer is' comes from, and where the raw-schema path is exposed to silent ambiguity that the ontology path structurally prevents.
accessibleSummary: A flow diagram with two parallel branches from the same starting question. The left branch queries a raw star schema directly: an NL2SQL model must infer table joins, business meaning, and filter definitions purely from column names and a prompt, with no published, shared definition to check against. The right branch queries through a Fabric IQ ontology: NL2Ontology constrains its generated query to the ontology's own published entity types, relationships, and rules. Both branches converge on a comparison node showing that the raw path can silently diverge in its answer depending on which developer built the prompt, while the ontology path is structurally forced to agree with every other consumer of the same ontology. A warning node covers the concrete failure mode: two teams' raw-schema agents answering 'how many active customers' differently with no way to reconcile the discrepancy.
longDescription: This is a flow diagram structured as two parallel paths from a shared starting point, converging on a comparison. Both paths start from the same natural-language business question. The left (raw) path shows an NL2SQL model reasoning directly over a star-schema's raw tables and columns, inferring business meaning without any published definition to constrain it against. The right (ontology) path shows NL2Ontology constraining its generated query to entity types, relationships, and rules the ontology has already published. The two paths converge at a comparison node that states the structural difference plainly: the raw path's answer is only as consistent as whichever prompt or developer built that specific query, while the ontology path's answer is guaranteed to agree with every other system built against the same ontology, because they all resolve through the same published definitions. A warning node grounds the raw path's risk in a concrete, real scenario — two independently built agents disagreeing on the definition of 'active customer.'

nodes.label: Business question
nodes.summary: The same natural-language question is the starting point for both paths compared in this diagram.
nodes.detail: A business user asks a plain-English question about a domain concept — for example, how many active customers exist, or which shipments breached a cold-chain rule. This diagram traces what happens to that same question along two different architectural paths: one against a raw star schema, one through a Fabric IQ ontology.
nodes.whyItMatters: Holding the question constant is what makes the two paths genuinely comparable — the difference in outcome comes entirely from what each path does with the same input, not from asking two different things.

inputs: A natural-language business question with no attached technical definition of its terms
processing: No processing yet — this is the shared starting point for both comparison branches
outputs: The identical question, forwarded down both the raw-schema path and the ontology path
drill.example: 'How many active customers do we have?' is asked twice — once against a raw star-schema NL2SQL agent, once against an ontology-grounded data agent — to compare what each returns and why.
controls: None at this node — it exists to hold the comparison fair
failureModes: Comparing two paths against subtly different questions and attributing the resulting difference to the wrong cause

nodes.label: NL2SQL over raw star schema
nodes.summary: An NL2SQL model infers joins, filters, and business meaning purely from column names and the prompt — no published definition to check against.
nodes.detail: Without a shared ontology layer, every business question posed to an AI system requires manual translation, by a domain expert, from raw tables and schemas into business concepts. A raw-schema NL2SQL path has no ontology to constrain it — the model's understanding of what 'active' or 'customer' means comes entirely from however that specific prompt, instruction set, or developer defined it for that specific agent.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the structural gap the ontology layer exists to close: nothing here prevents two different builders from encoding two different definitions of the same business term.

evidence.note: Without a shared ontology layer, AI systems are described as unfit for high-stakes decisions because every business question otherwise requires manual translation by a domain expert from raw tables/schemas into business concepts.

inputs: Raw star-schema table/column names, with no published business-term definitions
processing: Infer likely table joins from foreign-key-like column names
Infer a definition for ambiguous business terms (e.g. 'active') purely from prompt context or developer-supplied instructions
Generate a SQL query against the raw tables
outputs: A SQL query and answer whose definition of the business term is implicit and specific to this one build
drill.example: One team's NL2SQL agent defines 'active customer' as an order in the trailing 90 days, inferred from a comment in its own prompt — nothing published constrains that choice, and no other system can discover or reuse it.
controls: Prompt engineering and developer-supplied instructions — the only lever available, and it is per-agent, not shared
failureModes: A different developer building a second agent against the same tables and independently choosing a different definition for the same term

nodes.label: NL2Ontology over Fabric IQ ontology
nodes.summary: The generated query is constrained to entity types, relationships, and rules the ontology has already published.
nodes.detail: An ontology (preview) item defines core business entities, relationships, properties, rules, and actions, and exposes a natural-language query layer (NL2Ontology) that converts business questions into structured queries. NL2Ontology constrains the generated filters, joins, units, and validity windows to the definitions published in the ontology, rather than letting a model infer them freely from raw schema.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the structural guarantee the raw path lacks: the model is not allowed to invent its own definition of a business term on the fly, because NL2Ontology only ever resolves against what the ontology has already published.

evidence.note: An ontology (preview) item defines core business entities, relationships, properties, rules, and actions, and exposes a natural-language query layer (NL2Ontology) that converts business questions into structured queries.

NL2Ontology converts natural-language business questions into structured ontology queries and constrains the generated filters, joins, units, and validity windows to the definitions published in the ontology, rather than letting a model infer them freely from raw schema.

inputs: The ontology's published entity types, properties, relationships, and rules
processing: Parse the question against published ontology definitions only
Generate filters, joins, units, and validity windows constrained to those definitions
Reject or flag terms the ontology has not published a definition for
outputs: A structured query whose definition of the business term is the ontology's single published one, discoverable by every other consumer
drill.example: The same 'active customer' question resolves against the ontology's one published Customer entity rule — whatever that rule is, every agent and report built against this ontology gets the same answer.
controls: What gets published in the ontology's entity types, properties, and rules — the single point of control for the definition
failureModes: A question referencing a business concept the ontology hasn't modeled yet, which NL2Ontology cannot resolve without either failing or falling back to unconstrained inference

nodes.label: Comparison: per-build vs shared definition
nodes.summary: The raw path's answer depends on which build answered it; the ontology path's answer is the same no matter which consumer asks.
nodes.detail: Fabric IQ's stated benefits cluster around cross-domain reasoning, faster onboarding, and governance. Governance comes from enforcing consistent definitions across teams — the same mechanism that prevents onboarding friction also prevents different teams from quietly drifting into incompatible definitions of the same business concept. That governance benefit only exists because the ontology path resolves through one shared, published definition, while the raw-schema path resolves through however many independently-built prompts exist.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the entire argument for Fabric IQ made concrete: it isn't that raw NL2SQL is technically worse at generating SQL, it's that it has no mechanism to guarantee two different systems agree on what a business term means.

inputs: An answer from the raw NL2SQL path
An answer from the ontology-grounded path
Both to the same original question
processing: Compare whether the two answers agree
If they disagree, trace the raw path's answer back to whichever prompt/instructions produced its private definition
outputs: A structural explanation for why the ontology path is governable and the raw path is not, independent of whether this particular comparison happens to agree
drill.example: Both paths might coincidentally return the same number today; the difference only becomes visible when a second team builds a second raw-schema agent and gets a different number for the identical business term.
controls: Whether an organization standardizes on the ontology path for governed, cross-team business questions
failureModes: Assuming raw NL2SQL and ontology-grounded answers will always match because they happened to match in one test

nodes.label: Real failure: two teams, two definitions
nodes.summary: Different experts translating the same data into subtly different business meanings, with no way to reconcile.
nodes.detail: That manual-translation step doesn't scale, and it introduces exactly the kind of inconsistency — different experts translating the same underlying data into subtly different business meanings — that makes AI systems unreliable for high-stakes decisions. This is the concrete, real-world consequence of the raw-schema path shown on the left of this diagram: it is not a hypothetical risk, it is the documented reason Fabric IQ's ontology layer exists.
nodes.whyItMatters: An AI agent making a governed business decision on top of an inconsistent, undocumented definition is a decision made on unreliable grounds — this is a governance risk, not merely an engineering inconvenience.

evidence.note: That manual-translation step doesn't scale, and it introduces exactly the kind of inconsistency — different experts translating the same underlying data into subtly different business meanings — that makes AI systems unreliable for high-stakes decisions.

inputs: Two or more independently built raw-schema NL2SQL agents or reports over the same underlying tables
processing: Each builder infers a definition for an ambiguous business term with no shared reference to check against
No process exists to detect or reconcile the resulting divergence
outputs: Two systems that confidently give two different answers to what looks like the same question
drill.example: Finance's raw-schema report counts 'active customer' as having a non-cancelled subscription; a support team's raw-schema agent counts it as having logged in within 30 days — both are used in the same executive meeting with no one aware they disagree.
controls: Adopting a shared ontology (the right-hand path in this diagram) as the single source of definition truth for governed decisions
failureModes: Discovering the discrepancy only after a high-stakes decision has already been made on the disagreeing numbers
